lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Eight Actors, Eighty Days
lessons.description: Eason's episodic chase across continents: how eight actors tell a global story.
lessons.content_html:
A Novel Becomes a Race Against the Clock

Jules Verne published his adventure novel in 1872, at a moment when two technologies had just made circumnavigation in eighty days theoretically possible: the Suez Canal opened in 1869 and the American transcontinental railroad was completed in the same year. Verne imagined a precise English gentleman betting £20,000 at his gentlemen's club that he could complete the journey — and the result is a breathless chase spanning India, Hong Kong, Japan, San Francisco and the Atlantic. Laura Eason's 2013 stage adaptation, which premiered at the New Vic Theatre in Newcastle-under-Lyme in a theatre-in-the-round configuration, distils this chase into something even tighter: eight actors playing every role in the story, from Phileas Fogg himself to train conductors, customs officials, ship’s captains and a herd of elephants. Understanding the episodic structure of this adaptation is the starting point for all the staging and performance work that follows.

Key Fact

Eason’s adaptation premiered at the New Vic Theatre, Newcastle-under-Lyme in 2013, directed by Theresa Heskins, in a theatre-in-the-round configuration with a cast of eight actors multi-roling throughout.

Episodic Structure and the Chase Narrative

Where a linear play builds one continuous action through rising and falling tension, episodic structure links a series of self-contained scenes whose energy comes from momentum — the audience is always aware of time ticking down and distance to be crossed. Eason borrows this structure directly from Verne, who organised his novel as a series of geographical episodes: London, Paris, Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, Liverpool, London again. Each episode introduces new obstacles, new minor characters, and new opportunities for the eight-actor ensemble to transform themselves and the stage space. The play opens at the Reform Club opening, establishing Fogg’s precision and the terms of the wager, and closes in London with the apparent failure and then the extraordinary reveal of the international date line.

From a staging perspective, episodic structure creates specific demands. Each scene transition must be rapid — a shift of a chair, a change of costume accessory, a change of accent — and the performers and director must find ways to signal clearly to the audience that we have moved from one continent to another without slowing the pace. A director working on this play in an in-the-round space, as the original production did, must ensure that sightlines allow every audience member to see the key physical images from every angle: a tableau of the Reform Club, the arc of an elephant crossing the stage, the moment a train accelerates through the ensemble’s bodies.

A linear play (like The Crucible) builds one sustained dramatic question — will Proctor confess? — through escalating pressure in a single community. In contrast, Around the World in 80 Days has a fresh dramatic question in every new location: will Fogg catch the next departure? Will Fix succeed in detaining him? Will Passepartout survive his mishap in the Hong Kong opium-house scene? This episodic rhythm suits physical-theatre companies because each episode is essentially a self-contained performance problem: how do eight actors turn themselves into an Indian marketplace, a Japanese acrobat troupe, or a Native American war party on the transcontinental railway? The episodic form invites creativity in every transition rather than demanding sustained psychological realism in one fixed setting.

A common misconception students should avoid: episodic does not mean “random”. Every episode advances Fogg’s race against the clock, reveals character under pressure, and raises the comic and dramatic stakes. The structure is tight — the countdown creates tension across every episode, even when individual scenes are played for comedy.

Multi-Roling and the Ensemble as Engine

Multi-roling is not simply an economic decision in this play — it is the central theatrical pleasure. Eight performers play dozens of parts. One actor might be a Reform Club gentleman in the opening scene, a Suez customs officer ten minutes later, a Bombay merchant shortly after, and then a ship’s engineer in the Atlantic crossing. The audience’s delight comes partly from recognising the transformation and partly from the skill of the performer who makes each figure feel utterly distinct. For a student writing as a performer, this means that every minor character must be performed with precision: a distinct posture, a specific walk, a clear change of vocal pitch, pace or accent to mark the transition.

The eight-actor ensemble also creates the physical world of the play. Bodies become a steam engine (performers in a line, arms pumping in unison, voices creating a mechanical rhythm), an elephant (one actor as the body, others as legs, the whole image emerging from choreographed physical trust), or the heaving Atlantic (performers shifting weight in synchrony, creating a wave motion across the stage). This use of bodies-as-objects and object transformation is characteristic of companies like Complicite and Frantic Assembly, whose physical-theatre practice underpins Eason’s script.

Key Fact

The ensemble uses physical theatre to transform performers’ bodies into the world of the play — steam engines, ships, elephants, storms and crowds — making multi-roling and object transformation central staging methods rather than incidental features.

A significant student error is to treat this play as a costume drama requiring a literal, naturalistic set — a train carriage for the India scenes, a ship’s deck for the Atlantic, an Indian temple for the rescue of Aouda. In fact the play’s entire aesthetic is built on the idea that the imagination of performers and audience, not scenery, creates the world. A director who specifies a realistic Victorian set is misreading the form. Stylised staging is not a compromise here — it is the artistic intention. Chairs become railway carriages; rope becomes rigging; the ensemble’s coordinated movement becomes the ocean. Examiners reward students who understand this and who can describe how specific design choices support the transformation rather than substitute for it.

Narrated Transitions and Direct Address

Eason also employs a narration device: performers step out of the dramatic fiction to address the audience directly, setting the location, updating the countdown, and commenting on Fogg’s progress. This direct address functions similarly to Brecht’s use of a narrator in epic theatre — it frames the action, prevents the audience from losing themselves in pure empathy, and invites them to watch the storytelling as storytelling. From a design perspective, lighting transitions between dramatic scenes and narrator moments can be achieved with a sharp change of lighting state: for example, a warm, busy wash during action scenes and a tight top-light or single profile lantern on the narrator to isolate them from the rest of the stage, signalling to the audience that we have stepped outside the story.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to analyse the playwright’s intentions, the most common mistake is describing what happens in the play rather than explaining what the playwright wants the audience to think or feel at that moment. For a question about the episodic structure, always connect the structural choice to the audience experience: the episodic form keeps the clock ticking in the audience’s mind, creating a cumulative momentum that a linear form could not sustain. For extended staging questions, you must go beyond structure and identify concrete staging choices — how would you physically mark each scene transition? Which lighting state signals a new location? How does the ensemble move to signal the steam engine? Name specific moments and specific technical choices. “The lighting would change” scores in the Developing band; “a snap blackout followed by a cool blue wash from upstage cross-lights to suggest the open Atlantic” is the Mastering band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eason’s 2013 adaptation uses episodic structure to match Verne’s globe-trotting novel, creating a continuous ticking clock that connects every scene — eight actors, multi-roling throughout, are the engine of this structure.
  • Multi-roling and object transformation are central theatrical pleasures, not just economic choices: the ensemble creates trains, ships, elephants and storms through stylised physical theatre rather than realistic scenery.
  • Direct address narration frames the action, and a director’s choices about lighting state and staging configuration (in-the-round, ensuring sightlines for every audience member) shape how the audience experiences each episode.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason uses episodic structure and direct address narration to communicate the theme of time and the urgency of Fogg's wager to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses episodic structure as a deliberate choice to keep the countdown audible throughout the play, explaining that Eason intends each new episode to reset and increase the tension rather than resolve it. Direct address narration is analysed as a device that makes the audience co-witnesses of the clock ticking, positioning them as stakeholders in the wager. Concrete staging references are made (e.g. narrator stepping into a pool of light to update the audience on days remaining; blackout between episodes signalling time lost). The response considers how both methods together create a cumulative audience experience of urgency. A substantiated judgement is made about how effectively this communicates Verne's original theme.
Secure: Most of the above is present; at least one staging reference is concrete; the link between structure and audience experience is generally accurate.
Developing: Relevant points about the structure are made but staging implications are generic or absent; the connection to the theme of time is implied rather than analysed.
Emerging: The response describes what happens in the play or lists features of episodic structure without explaining their effect on the audience.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Around the World in 80 Days. Discuss how you would use the staging space, the ensemble's physical skills, and lighting and sound design to bring the Reform Club opening scene and the first departure from London to life. Refer to specific staging choices across at least three theatrical elements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response makes specific choices across multiple theatrical elements with clear justification for each. Staging configuration is discussed (e.g. in-the-round: Reform Club chairs arranged centre stage, Fogg placed upstage centre to dominate sightlines from all sides). Ensemble physical work is described precisely (e.g. the Reform Club gentlemen creating a formal tableau, rigid posture and synchronised movement to signal Victorian social constraint; the physical shift to the first locomotive created by performers forming a line downstage, arms pumping, a percussive soundscape built from breath and stamp). Lighting choices are named (e.g. warm amber wash for the Reform Club interior; a sharp blackout and then a cooler blue-white chase of side-lights to suggest movement as Fogg departs). Sound design is referenced (e.g. ticking clock underscoring Fogg's opening speech; a steam whistle cue as the journey begins). Every choice is linked to the play's themes (precision, momentum, the ticking clock). A directorial intention is stated and sustained throughout.
Secure: Most elements are covered; choices are mostly concrete; directorial intention is generally clear; at least two theatrical disciplines addressed in detail.
Developing: Some staging ideas are present but choices are described generically (e.g. 'the lighting would be dramatic'); fewer than two disciplines addressed with specific detail.
Emerging: The response lists ideas without explaining how they would work on stage or what effect they would create for the audience.

lessons.title: Characters: Fogg, Passepartout and a Cast of Many
lessons.description: Fogg's eccentric precision, Passepartout's energy, Fix's pursuit and Aouda's arc.
lessons.content_html:
The Four Major Characters

Around the World in 80 Days has a small core company at its dramatic centre, surrounded by the dozens of minor characters produced by the eight-actor ensemble. Understanding each major character’s function — and the precise physical and vocal choices a performer might make — is essential for the extended-response questions you will encounter in the exam. Let’s take them in turn.

Phileas Fogg: the Still Centre

Fogg is one of the most unusual protagonists in the set-play list. Where most leads carry the play through visible emotional change — Proctor's moral disintegration, Mickey's rage-filled final scene — Fogg’s dramatic function is almost the opposite. His stillness is the comic engine. Every obstacle that throws Passepartout into comic crisis simply registers on Fogg as a minor inconvenience to be noted in his schedule. A performer playing Fogg should resist the temptation to play him as broadly comic. Instead, the performance choices are rooted in understatement: an upright posture, precise and unhurried movement, a measured vocal delivery with minimal variation in pitch — and then, in the moments that matter (the rescue of Aouda, the final London revelation), a tiny shift of vocal warmth or physical openness that carries enormous weight precisely because of the stillness that surrounds it.

From a design perspective, Fogg’s visual identity is equally precise. A costume designer might use a dark Victorian frock coat, waistcoat and pocket watch as the anchoring constant — the one costume that never changes throughout the journey while everything around him transforms. This contrast between Fogg’s fixed costume and the constantly shifting proxemics of the ensemble around him gives the audience a visual anchor in every new location.

Key Fact

Fogg’s stillness and emotional restraint are his defining performance quality. The comedy arises from the gap between his unflustered calm and the chaos erupting around him — and this gap is entirely dependent on Passepartout’s energy as contrast.

Jean Passepartout: the Audience's Way In

If Fogg is the still centre, Passepartout is the kinetic perimeter. The French valet functions as the audience’s emotional guide through the journey: he worries when we worry, panics when the plan threatens to unravel, and celebrates when the adventure turns in their favour. A performer playing Passepartout has much greater physical and vocal range to work with than the performer playing Fogg. Blocking choices for Passepartout should be energetic and reactive — he might move frequently across the stage, use larger gestures, speak with more variation in pitch and pace, and respond visibly in his body to each new development. His relationship to the audience can include moments of direct comedy: a wide-eyed look to the audience when Fogg announces the next leg of the journey, a physical double-take, a sudden stillness of comic alarm.

Crucially, examiners reward students who understand that Passepartout and Fogg’s comedy is entirely dependent on their contrast. If a performer plays Fogg as energetic, the play loses its engine. If a performer plays Passepartout as restrained, the comic double-act collapses. The proxemics between them — Fogg typically upstage centre or slightly elevated, Passepartout closer to the audience at downstage centre — reinforces the status difference while keeping Passepartout as the audience’s primary point of identification.

Consider the moment in the play when Fogg announces each new leg of the journey after an obstacle has threatened to derail the schedule. As a performer playing Fogg: hold an upright posture, speak the announcement in a measured pace with a level pitch, and allow a brief pause before delivering the key line — the pause creates audience anticipation. As a performer playing Passepartout in the same moment: stand in contrast — slightly hunched from exertion or anxiety, reacting visibly in the shoulders and face. When Fogg delivers his line, allow a beat of stunned stillness followed by a physical release of breath that communicates relief or disbelief. This is the double-act mechanism at work: Fogg’s understatement amplifies Passepartout’s reaction, and Passepartout’s reaction amplifies the comedy of Fogg’s stillness.

Inspector Fix: the Pursuing Antagonist

Fix is a Scotland Yard detective who is convinced Fogg is the perpetrator of a bank robbery. He pursues the party from the Suez Canal onwards, attempting to delay Fogg at each stop so that a warrant can catch up with him. Fix creates dramatic irony: the audience knows Fogg is innocent, Fix does not, and this gap generates comedy as well as tension. A performer playing Fix must walk a line between genuine threat (he has the legal power to detain Fogg) and comic obsession (his certainty is transparently wrong, and increasingly desperate). Vocally, Fix might employ a slightly faster pace than Fogg — suggesting agitation beneath a professional exterior — and physical choices that place him in the gaps between the main party: always slightly upstage, slightly to one side, watching from upstage in a way that signals surveillance without interrupting the main action.

Aouda: from Rescued to Active

Aouda is the young Indian woman rescued by Fogg from a dangerous situation in India. Students often under-write her, treating her as a passive figure — rescued, grateful, silent. This is a significant misconception. While Verne’s original novel is a product of its time in its portrayal of Indian women, Eason’s adaptation (and the performance traditions that have grown around it) understand Aouda as someone whose arc moves from shock and vulnerability in her first scenes to active participation in the company as the journey continues. By the final London scenes she is part of the decision-making group, not simply an observer. A performer playing Aouda should track this arc physically: an initial containedness — quieter movement, closer proximity to Fogg as her protector — gradually opening into a more assured spatial presence, with more confident eye contact with both other characters and the audience, as her trust in the company grows.

Key Fact

Aouda moves from a rescued, vulnerable figure in the India scenes to an active member of Fogg’s company by the London ending. A performer should track this arc through changes in posture, spatial confidence and eye contact across the play.

The Multi-Roled Ensemble: Character Through Transformation

Beyond the four core characters, the eight-actor ensemble plays every other role in the play — the Reform Club wager-makers, the Suez customs official, the Bombay merchant, ship captains, train conductors, Native American warriors, Yokohama acrobats, and more. Each transformation requires the performer to signal a new character quickly and clearly. The technique is not naturalistic psychology — there is no time for a Stanislavskian interior journey into each minor character’s backstory. Instead, the physical-theatre vocabulary of the play demands clear gestus — a posture or gesture that instantly communicates the character’s social function and status. The Suez customs official stands with an officious squared-up posture, arms slightly out to signal authority; the Yokohama acrobat drops into a low centre of gravity with loose, ready limbs. These images are legible to the whole audience in an in-the-round configuration because they read from every angle.

A common student error is to describe minor characters as “the same performers in different costumes.” In Eason’s play, the theatrical pleasure of multi-roling comes from the distinctiveness of each transformation. The skill is in the precision of the gestus — how fully and quickly a performer can inhabit a completely different physical and vocal register. When writing as a performer for the exam, always specify what changes: the posture, the pace of movement, the pitch or accent of the voice. “The performer would act differently” scores no marks; “the performer would shift from Passepartout’s loose, reactive physicality to a squared, authoritative stillness and a more clipped English accent for the Reform Club gentleman” scores well.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark performer questions on this play, the most common error is writing about what the character is feeling without translating that into specific vocal and physical choices. An examiner cannot give marks for “I would show that Passepartout is frightened.” You must say: how would you show it? Name the vocal quality (e.g. a raised pitch, a faster pace, a mid-phrase pause as if catching breath), the physical choice (e.g. a backward step towards the edge of the stage, slightly raised shoulders, a hand reaching towards Fogg before being withdrawn), and the spatial relationship (e.g. pulling away from Fix’s position upstage to place more distance between them). For every character in this play, think in terms of contrast: how do your choices for Fogg differ from your choices for Passepartout? How do your choices for Fix differ from the choices for Fogg? Contrast and specificity are the keys to the higher bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fogg’s stillness and emotional restraint are deliberate performance choices that create the comic double-act with Passepartout — playing him energetically would destroy the play’s central mechanism.
  • Aouda’s arc from rescued vulnerability to active company member must be tracked physically across the play; under-writing her is a common exam mistake.
  • Minor characters in the ensemble require precise gestus — a clear physical attitude that communicates social function and status instantly, readable from every angle in an in-the-round configuration.

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Jean Passepartout in the moment when Fogg announces that they must immediately depart for Yokohama despite a setback, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make. Refer to one specific staging choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response makes precise, concrete vocal choices (e.g. a rapidly rising pitch as Passepartout processes the news, followed by a mid-sentence break — a vocal pause that communicates stunned disbelief before the rush of anxious speech; volume rising slightly, pace increasing as panic builds). Physical choices are equally specific (e.g. an initial involuntary step backward at the announcement, shoulders rising toward the ears in a physical gesture of alarm; hands briefly raised before dropping as Passepartout visibly decides to comply). Staging choice is named and justified (e.g. Passepartout positioned downstage centre, closer to the audience than Fogg, so that his reaction is the audience's primary lens into the moment; turning briefly to face the audience before snapping back to Fogg communicates that Passepartout, like the audience, finds the plan absurd). The response explains how these choices create comedy and audience empathy.
Secure: Both vocal and physical choices are present and generally concrete; staging reference is included; the effect on the audience is described.
Developing: Relevant ideas but either vocal or physical choices are generic (e.g. 'I would look shocked'); staging choice absent or vague.
Emerging: Describes feeling without translating into specific performance choices.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a director might stage the moment Aouda first appears, in the India scenes, to communicate her vulnerability and the play's moral stakes to the audience. Refer to proxemics, lighting and at least one performer choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response articulates a clear directorial vision for the moment. Proxemics are used with precision — for example, Aouda is placed centre stage, surrounded by the ensemble, whose physical mass and proximity communicate threat without any dialogue; Fogg and Passepartout are positioned upstage, initially outside the scene, so the audience perceives the danger before the protagonists do. Performer choices for Aouda are specific: a still, contained posture, arms close to the body, limited movement communicating constraint; voice initially silent or near-silent, communicating shock. Lighting is named and justified: a tight warm special on Aouda isolating her from a cooler, more diffuse wash on the ensemble around her, creating a visual focal point and generating audience sympathy for her position. The response connects these choices to the play's broader concern with what Fogg's adventure means for the people he encounters. Sound design might also be referenced (e.g. a soundscape mixing the ensemble's voices with distant music to create the atmosphere of the location, contrasting with silence around Aouda's moments of stillness). A directorial intention is clearly stated and the choices are weighed against each other.
Secure: At least three theatrical elements are addressed with mostly concrete choices; directorial intention is generally clear; proxemics, lighting and performer choices are all present.
Developing: Some staging ideas are present; fewer than three elements addressed in concrete detail; the connection to the play's moral stakes is implied rather than developed.
Emerging: Lists staging ideas without explaining how they work together or what effect they create for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason constructs the relationship between Fogg and Passepartout to create comic effect and communicate meaning to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses Fogg and Passepartout as a deliberately constructed double-act, explaining that Eason intends the contrast between Fogg's stillness and Passepartout's energy to be the primary comic mechanism. The analysis goes beyond description to consider what the playwright wants the audience to take from this dynamic: Fogg's calm in the face of chaos communicates Victorian stoicism and eccentricity as both admirable and absurd; Passepartout's panic functions as a realistic human mirror for the audience, who can laugh at what Fogg refuses to acknowledge. Concrete staging references are made — for example, how blocking choices that separate them spatially allow the audience to read both reactions simultaneously, with Fogg's stillness upstage amplifying Passepartout's movement downstage. A considered judgement is reached about how this character dynamic communicates something broader about the play's themes.
Secure: The double-act dynamic is identified and mostly analysed; at least one staging reference; the link to broader meaning is present.
Developing: The relationship is described with some relevant observation, but analysis is limited to surface description rather than playwright's intention.
Emerging: Describes the characters separately rather than analysing the relationship between them.

lessons.title: Themes: Time, Empire and Adventure
lessons.description: Victorian steam, schedules and global mastery — and what a modern stage can say about empire.
lessons.content_html:
Three Interlocking Themes

Around the World in 80 Days asks three related questions that operate simultaneously: what does time mean? What does the British Empire mean? And what is adventure? These are not separate compartments in the play — they are woven together in every scene. Fogg’s obsession with the schedule is inseparable from the Victorian culture of industrial precision that made British imperialism possible. The places Fogg travels through — India, Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, America — are the map of British and European colonial reach in 1872. And the sense of adventure that Verne’s novel celebrates is, in a modern production, always in dialogue with the question of whose world is being adventured through. A post-colonial reading of the play does not require abandoning the adventure — it requires understanding what the adventure was for.

Time, Schedule and Victorian Punctuality

The wager itself — £20,000 on an eighty-day circumnavigation — is a meditation on industrial time. The Suez Canal and the transcontinental railroad had made the journey mathematically possible; Fogg tests this possibility against the precision of timetables, departure slots and scheduled connections. For a Victorian audience, this celebration of schedule was a celebration of modernity itself: steam, rail, and the telegraph had compressed the world into measurable units. From a staging perspective, the theme of time can be physicalised in many ways. A sound designer might create a soundscape in which a ticking clock is woven underneath every scene — barely audible at the start but gradually louder as the eighty days compress. The rhythm of the ensemble’s physical work — the mechanical precision of the steam engine sequence, the synchronised tick of the Reform Club gentlemen consulting their watches — gives the theme physical form.

Key Fact

The theme of time is not just a narrative fact — it is a design opportunity. A ticking clock soundscape, growing in volume as the eighty days diminish, physicalises the countdown and creates cumulative tension for the audience regardless of which scene they are watching.

The British Empire and the Colonial Gaze

Verne’s novel is a product of the imperial imagination: the world outside Europe exists primarily as backdrop for Fogg’s determination and Passepartout’s comedy. The Indian characters are largely incidental; Aouda is defined initially by her need to be rescued; the Native American attack on the transcontinental railroad is a thrilling obstacle rather than a historically contextualised act of resistance. A 21st-century production cannot present this material uncritically without becoming uncomfortable in ways that serve neither the play nor the students watching it. Eason’s script and the production tradition around it find a range of ways to address this: the ensemble’s awareness of each new location can be performed with genuine curiosity rather than condescension; Aouda’s arc gives an Indian woman agency in the second half of the play; and design choices about costume and soundscape can represent the cultures Fogg passes through with specificity and respect rather than as a generic “exotic.”

Examiners reward students who acknowledge this tension and engage with it as a production question rather than a moral verdict. The question is not “is this play racist?” but “how would you, as a director or designer, stage the Indian marketplace scene so that the audience engages with India as a real, complex place rather than a colourful backdrop for Fogg’s journey?” This is a staging and design question, and it has specific, assessable answers.

Consider three specific design approaches a modern director might take. First, in soundscape: a sound designer could build the Indian marketplace scene from authentic Indian musical textures — a tabla rhythm, a specific raga mode played on sitar — rather than a generic “Eastern” musical cliché. This communicates that the production has engaged with the real culture rather than Verne’s impression of it. Second, in costume: ensemble members playing Indian characters might have specific, researched costume elements — a particular fabric, a specific garment form — that communicate cultural identity with precision. Third, in performance: the ensemble members might play Indian characters with the same specificity and gestus care they bring to the Reform Club gentlemen, resisting the temptation to use Indian scenes as pure physical spectacle. None of these choices requires rewriting the play; all of them require careful, thoughtful production design.

Adventure, Comedy and the Audience

The third major theme — adventure — is the play’s most immediate emotional register. Audiences come to have fun, to follow a chase, to laugh at Passepartout and admire Fogg. The adventure genre has specific theatrical vocabulary: pace, physical spectacle, comic reversal, the near-miss. Eason honours this by keeping every episode moving, by using the tableau sparingly for high-impact moments (the rescue of Aouda, the final reveal), and by placing the ensemble’s physical virtuosity at the centre of each new location. A director working on this play must balance the adventure’s energy with the moments of stillness that give the themes weight. The London ending — in which Fogg believes he has failed, then discovers through the international date line that he has succeeded — requires a complete tonal shift: from the silence of apparent defeat to the joy of unexpected victory. Blackout followed by an entirely different lighting state can serve this tonal pivot: a deep silence and near-darkness for the apparent failure, then a warmth of light and sound flooding back in as the date line is revealed.

Key Fact

The London ending demands a tonal pivot: Fogg’s apparent failure followed by the date line revelation. A blackout and silence mark the low point; a warm lighting wash and sound flooding back in mark the turn — a simple but powerful staging choice that communicates the emotional reversal.

Students sometimes feel that the “correct” answer to colonial themes is to stage the play as a critique of Fogg or Verne. This is too simple. The play’s joy and energy come from the adventure; a production that turns the comedy into a lecture about imperialism will lose its audience. The more sophisticated production approach — and the one examiners reward — is to use design and performance choices to add depth and specificity to the non-European characters and locations, so that the world Fogg travels through feels genuinely inhabited by real people with their own dignity, rather than as a backdrop. This does not require condemning Fogg; it requires the production to be aware of what Verne’s novel couldn’t see, and to quietly, visually correct that blind spot through skilled design.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark analyse-intentions questions on themes, the most common mistake is describing the theme — “the play is about time” — without analysing what the playwright wants the audience to think, feel or understand about that theme at a specific moment. Always connect the theme to a named staging moment and to an audience effect. For questions about the colonial theme, you will gain marks by showing that you understand this as a production and design question, not just a literary one — explain how a director would stage a specific scene to handle this theme, not just that the theme is “complicated.” For 20-mark extended staging questions, use the themes as the backbone of your directorial choices: every design decision should serve one of the themes (time, empire, adventure) and your answer should make this clear.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three major themes — time, empire and adventure — are inseparable: Fogg’s schedule-obsession, the colonial geography of the journey, and the adventure genre’s energy all operate together in every scene.
  • The colonial theme is a production and design question: examiners reward students who describe specific staging choices that give the cultures Fogg passes through dignity and specificity, not students who simply note that Verne was writing in the Victorian era.
  • The London ending’s tonal pivot from failure to joy is a lighting and sound design opportunity: blackout and silence for the low point, a warm wash and returning sound for the revelation — a simple choice that communicates emotional reversal.

lessons.title: Context: Verne in 1872, Eason in 2013
lessons.description: The Victorian novel, its 19th-century travel craze, and how a modern adaptation reframes it.
lessons.content_html:
Two Worlds, One Journey

Around the World in 80 Days exists in two historical moments simultaneously. Jules Verne published the novel in 1872, feeding a Victorian appetite for global adventure at the precise moment when industrial technology had made such adventure feasible. Laura Eason’s stage adaptation premiered in 2013 at a theatre in the north of England, for a 21st-century audience well aware of what empire had meant and where the “adventure” of Victorian global reach had led. Understanding both contexts is essential not because examiners will ask you to reproduce biographical facts, but because context shapes every staging choice a modern production might make — from the style of the physical theatre to the way the ensemble performs the non-European characters. Both Verne’s world and Eason’s inform what happens on stage.

Jules Verne and the Victorian Moment

Jules Verne (1828–1905) was a French novelist and one of the founders of adventure fiction as a genre. He was fascinated by science and technology, and his novels are populated by engineers, explorers, submarines and balloons — the machines of a world in which human ingenuity was transforming the possible. Around the World in 80 Days was published in 1872, serialised in a French newspaper before appearing as a novel. It arrived at a specific historical junction: the Suez Canal had opened in 1869, dramatically shortening the sea journey between Europe and India; the American transcontinental railroad, also completed in 1869, had linked the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. Together these two engineering achievements made Verne’s premise credible — a journey that would have taken six months was now theoretically achievable in eighty days.

The novel’s popularity was also driven by a specifically Victorian cultural obsession with time. The Great Exhibition of 1851 had celebrated industrial progress and the mastery of nature through technology; by the 1870s, standardised railway time was replacing local time across Britain, the telegraph was sending messages faster than any human traveller, and the world was being divided into predictable time zones. Fogg’s devotion to his schedule is not a character quirk — it is a satirical portrait of Victorian industrial modernity, where the precision of the timetable had become a cultural value.

Key Fact

Verne wrote his novel in 1872, shortly after the Suez Canal (1869) and the transcontinental railroad (1869) made circumnavigation in 80 days theoretically possible. The Victorian obsession with time, schedules and industrial progress gave Fogg’s character its cultural meaning.

The Novel's Colonial Assumptions

Verne’s novel is a product of French and European imperial culture. The world outside Europe functions as spectacular terrain for Fogg’s determination. India, China, Japan and America appear as a series of exotic episodes, each offering a different flavour of drama or comedy. Verne writes with genuine curiosity about these places, but his gaze is consistently that of the European traveller: the cultures he describes are observed from the outside. This is not a unique failing of Verne — it was the dominant mode of 19th-century travel writing, in which the world was divided into the civilised (European) traveller and the colourful (non-European) spectacle. A modern student reading the novel will notice this immediately; a modern director staging the play must decide how to handle it.

Victorian adventure fiction as a genre typically features: a Western (usually British or French) protagonist whose ingenuity and stoicism are tested by the world; a loyal, comic companion who provides the audience’s emotional reaction; a series of exotic locations each with its own distinctive “character”; and a resolution that confirms the protagonist’s superiority through success. Verne’s novel fits this template closely, which is why Eason’s adaptation can engage with both the pleasure of the genre and the questions a modern audience brings to it. The physical-theatre form Eason writes for — eight actors explicitly constructing the world — is itself a kind of comment on the genre: by making the construction visible, the production invites the audience to watch the storytelling as storytelling, rather than being absorbed unquestioningly into the colonial adventure. This is the same principle as alienation effect in epic theatre: the ensemble’s visible transformations remind the audience that they are watching a story, not experiencing reality.

Laura Eason and the 2013 Stage Adaptation

Laura Eason is an American playwright, known in Britain for her work with the New Vic Theatre in Newcastle-under-Lyme. Her adaptation was commissioned specifically for the New Vic’s in-the-round space, directed by Theresa Heskins. This matters for staging: an in-the-round space requires a very different approach from a proscenium arch. There is no “upstage” as a place of exit or hiding; there is no wing space for surprise entrances; every costume change, every physical transformation, every blocking choice must work from every angle. The play Eason wrote is inseparable from this production context: the episodic multi-roling structure, the physical-theatre vocabulary, the use of minimal set and maximum performer ingenuity, all emerge from the demands of that space.

Eason’s adaptation is firmly in the tradition of physical theatre. The influence of companies like Complicite (founded 1983) and Frantic Assembly (founded 1994) is visible in the script’s demands: performers are asked to become not just multiple characters but multiple objects and environments. This ensemble physical-theatre tradition sits comfortably alongside the Brechtian concept of the visible storyteller — the performer who steps out to narrate, to comment, to address the audience directly, making the theatrical fiction visible rather than concealing it behind a naturalistic fourth wall.

Key Fact

Eason’s script draws on the physical-theatre traditions of Complicite (founded 1983) and Frantic Assembly (founded 1994), whose ensemble work — object transformation, bodies-as-environments, ensemble storytelling — underpins the play’s staging demands.

A student who understands both historical contexts can answer a context question with precision. For example: a 12-mark question asking how the historical context shapes a director’s choices for the India scenes might draw on three facts — (1) Verne wrote these scenes from a colonial gaze; (2) Eason adapted the play for a post-colonial 21st-century audience; (3) the physical-theatre form (visible transformation, ensemble storytelling) allows a modern production to handle this material critically without pausing the adventure. The directorial choice that follows from this context might be: the ensemble perform Indian characters with specific, researched gestus — a particular posture, a specific movement quality — that communicates genuine cultural specificity, not a tourist’s impression. This is a contextually informed staging choice, which is exactly what examiners reward at the highest band.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Context questions require you to connect historical or theatrical facts directly to staging choices — not simply to list them. A common mistake is writing two paragraphs about Victorian history and Verne’s biography and then adding “this would affect the director’s choices” without specifying how. The examiner needs to see the link made explicit: “Because Verne wrote from within a colonial culture, a modern director staging the India scenes would need to make deliberate choices to give Indian characters their own specificity — for example, using a researched gestus for each character rather than generic physical caricature.” That is a contextually grounded staging answer. For the 12-mark analyse-intentions question, always move from context to intention to specific staging choice to audience effect — four steps, every time.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Verne wrote in 1872 when the Suez Canal and the transcontinental railroad had made circumnavigation in 80 days newly possible — Fogg’s schedule-obsession reflects Victorian industrial culture, not personal eccentricity.
  • Eason’s 2013 adaptation for the New Vic’s in-the-round space draws on the physical-theatre traditions of Complicite and Frantic Assembly — the in-the-round configuration directly shapes the play’s staging demands.
  • Understanding both historical contexts allows a director to make informed choices about how to handle Verne’s colonial gaze — using gestus, costume and soundscape to give non-European characters specificity and dignity.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Multi-roling, Mime and Storytelling
lessons.description: How eight actors become elephants, trains and crowds through physical theatre and narration.
lessons.content_html:
The Challenge: One World, Eight Actors

Laura Eason’s stage adaptation of Jules Verne’s novel asks a small ensemble to create an entire planet. Fogg’s journey crosses three continents, dozens of locations, and involves dozens of incidental characters — customs officials, ship’s captains, train conductors, Yokohama acrobats and one very large elephant. With a cast of typically eight, every performer must be skilled in multi-roling: stepping out of a minor part, shedding an accent or a hat, and stepping instantly into another. The play’s pleasure lies in watching this transformation happen live, in front of the audience, with no apology and no disguise.

Understanding these dramatic methods is essential for exam-style questions. Examiners want to see that you recognise why Eason chose this form, not just that the cast is small. The form makes the world feel vast and the journey feel kinetic — qualities a naturalistic production with a large cast and scene-changes could never achieve.

Key Fact

Eason’s adaptation uses multi-roling, mime, direct address narration, object transformation and ensemble physical theatre as its core dramatic methods. Together they let eight actors tell a story that spans the globe.

Narration and Direct Address

One of the production’s most important tools is direct address. Company members step forward to narrate transitions between scenes, update the audience on the days remaining, or comment on Fogg’s progress. This has two effects: it keeps the racing pace alive (no long scene-change during which energy drains away), and it recruits the audience as fellow travellers tracking the wager in real time.

Narration here is not passive. A performer narrating a train journey is also simultaneously performing it — their voice creates the soundscape while their body mimes the carriage, so the boundaries between “telling” and “showing” dissolve. This is ensemble storytelling at its most efficient. The technique owes a debt to practitioners such as Complicite, whose work since the 1980s has made the narrator—performer a central figure in physical theatre.

A common student error is to treat Eason’s ensemble form as a practical limitation — “there aren’t enough actors for a big cast.” This misses the point entirely. Eason chose this form deliberately because the experience of watching actors transform — from a train conductor to an elephant’s front legs to a Reform Club gentleman — creates theatrical energy that a naturalistic production cannot. The rapid role-switching mirrors the dizzying speed of Fogg’s journey. Examiners reward students who understand that the form is the meaning.

Mime and Physical Theatre

Mime is the engine of the production’s scene-setting. Where a naturalistic production would build a set, this company uses bodies. In the journey through India on elephant-back, the ensemble arranges itself to suggest the rhythm and sway of a large animal — one or two performers may form the front legs, others the haunches, while Fogg and Passepartout “ride” on top. The physical precision demanded of the company is equivalent to that of a dance piece.

Similarly, the crossing of the snowy American plains by train sees the ensemble arranged in rows of chairs, collectively swaying as the “carriage” accelerates. A performer at the front enacts the engine’s motion. The audience reads these configurations instantly. The vocabulary draws on the physical theatre tradition associated with Frantic Assembly and Complicite: the body is a flexible instrument capable of representing any object or environment with the right training and ensemble trust.

Key Fact

In this play, mime is not a fallback for missing props — it is the primary visual language. The audience’s imagination is recruited as a co-creator: they read a row of sway-and-jostle bodies as a train because the physical rhythm is unmistakably right.

Object Transformation

Object transformation is the third pillar of this production’s method. Chairs become railway carriages or the pews of a Reform Club; a length of rope becomes the rigging of a ship; a cane becomes a walking stick and then a conductor’s baton and then a rifle. The audience learns to interpret these transformations rapidly, partly because the physical use of the object teaches them what it “is” at any given moment.

This technique demands that performers commit fully. A chair is only a railway carriage if the performer sitting in it behaves exactly as they would in a moving train. The physical life — the sway, the grip on an imaginary armrest, the gaze out of an invisible window — persuades the audience. Break the physical logic and the fiction collapses. This requirement for total physical commitment is a core principle of physical theatre.

As a performer playing one of the ensemble in the elephant sequence, you might hold a low-to-the-ground posture, knees slightly bent, arms loose at the sides to suggest bulk. Your rhythm would synchronise with the other “legs” of the elephant — a slow, deliberate, four-count sway. Vocally, you would be silent: the physical work carries the scene. Your proxemics to the other ensemble members are tight — within touching distance — to suggest you are one creature rather than separate performers.

As a lighting designer, you might use a warm amber lighting special from a high angle to suggest the heat of the Indian sun. A gobo projecting dappled leaf-shadow patterns could suggest jungle canopy without a single physical piece of set. The warm wash would contrast with the cooler, greyer light used in London, immediately orientating the audience in a different part of the world.

Fast Costume Changes and Comic Timing

Multi-roling also demands a distinctive costume strategy. The production typically uses a base layer for each performer — a neutral Victorian suit or simple rehearsal costume — onto which accessories are layered rapidly: a hat, a badge, an accent, a way of walking. The base layer plus accessories system means a change from Reform Club gentleman to Indian customs official takes seconds rather than minutes.

Alongside this runs one of the production’s most important performance demands: comic timing. The play’s humour depends on the contrast between Fogg’s absolute stillness — his refusal to be rattled by any obstacle — and Passepartout’s physical and emotional expressiveness. Fogg’s stillness is the comic engine: it sets up a straight line against which Passepartout’s energy lands. Examiners reward students who understand that Fogg’s restraint is as much a performance choice as Passepartout’s flamboyance.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When you are asked to analyse intentions for a 12-mark question on this play, the most common error is to describe what happens rather than analysing why Eason chose this dramatic method and what effect it creates for the audience. Ask yourself: what does multi-roling make the audience feel? (Excitement, a sense of the world’s variety, admiration for the company.) What would be lost if a naturalistic cast played each character? (Speed, the theatrical pleasure of transformation, the sense that the play celebrates the act of storytelling itself.) Pin every point to a specific moment and a specific effect on the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Multi-roling, mime, direct address narration and object transformation are Eason’s core dramatic methods — they allow eight performers to create a globe-spanning world and are central to the play’s theatrical identity.
  • Narration collapses the boundary between telling and showing: the narrating performer is simultaneously performing the action, keeping pace alive and recruiting the audience as fellow travellers.
  • Comic timing — particularly the contrast between Fogg’s stillness and Passepartout’s energy — is a performance choice, not an accident; examiners reward students who analyse it as a deliberate method with a specific effect on the audience.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: A World on a Bare Stage
lessons.description: How chairs, rope and lighting transform into trains, ships and continents on a bare stage.
lessons.content_html:
Designing a World Without a Set

Eason’s stage adaptation was conceived for theatre in the round at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme. That original configuration shapes every design decision: there is no back wall to hang flats on, no single “front” to place a painted landscape. Everything must work from all angles. This forces the production into a minimalist aesthetic where objects, light and bodies carry the entire scenic burden — and that turns out to be the production’s greatest creative asset.

For a GCSE Drama student, this unit is a masterclass in how minimal scenography can actually communicate more than a fully realised naturalistic set. When the audience watches the company convert four chairs into a railway carriage, they are not passive observers — they are actively co-creating the fiction. The designer’s job is to give them just enough information so that their imagination completes the picture.

Key Fact

The production typically uses chairs as railway carriages, rope as ship rigging and canes as multiple tools — each transformation is achieved through precise physical use by the performer, not through visual trickery.

Set Design: The Empty Space as Possibility

The set designer’s first decision is stage configuration and levels. A production of this play that uses a central raised platform for the Reform Club gives Fogg an immediate visual authority: he is literally above the world he is about to conquer. When Passepartout operates at floor level, the contrast in levels communicates their relationship instantly, before a word is spoken.

Across the episodic structure, the only constants are a table and a set of chairs that can be reconfigured per scene. A row of chairs placed upstage and angled slightly can become the viewing gallery of the Reform Club; the same chairs rotated and placed downstage become a train carriage hurtling across America. The speed of these reconfigurations is part of the show’s theatrical language — an audience that sees chairs moved quickly learns to read those moves as scene changes and accepts the new location immediately.

A persistent student misconception is to suggest a large scenic elephant as the design solution for the India sequence. This misses the form the play is written for. Productions use puppet elephants or pure physical theatre (ensemble bodies) precisely because the play’s style is anti-naturalistic. Suggesting a painted or mechanised elephant in an exam answer signals that you have misread the genre. Examiners reward students who suggest stylised physical solutions consistent with the ensemble aesthetic — for example, a puppet elephant built collaboratively by the company using poles, fabric and collective movement, or pure ensemble mime.

Lighting Design: Painting the Globe

Because the set is minimal, the lighting designer carries enormous scenic responsibility. Each new location must be painted in light. A warm amber wash from a high angle creates the heat of India; a cold blue wash from the sides suggests the Atlantic crossing in winter; a neutral, slightly grey top light places us in foggy London. Lighting wash choices are the quickest way to transport an audience across continents.

More specific effects come from lantern choices. A profile lantern can be used to throw a hard-edged spotlight onto Fogg at the moment of the wager — isolating him from the Reform Club chatter as if the rest of the world has receded. A gobo of moving water patterns projected from above transforms the bare stage floor into the surface of the ocean for the Atlantic crossing. These specific design choices communicate location and mood simultaneously without a single piece of scenery being added.

Key Fact

Lighting transitions replace scene changes in this production. The move from a warm amber wash (India) to a cold blue wash (the Atlantic) is a design shorthand that takes less than ten seconds and instantly relocates the audience without a single piece of furniture being moved.

Sound Design: A Soundscape Around the World

The soundscape is equally important. Train whistles, steam hiss, ship bells, the call to prayer from a minaret, Yokohama street noise and the rhythmic clatter of railway track can all be designed into the production’s score. The sound designer has two main tools: diegetic sounds (those the characters would hear — the steam engine’s release of pressure) and non-diegetic underscore (a rising orchestral phrase as Fogg’s train accelerates, unheard by Fogg but felt by the audience).

Some productions interpolate live music — a pianist in the corner, a percussionist tracking the journey — which adds the additional layer of music-hall theatricality that the play’s comic tradition invites. The sound of a music-hall piano underscoring a chase sequence immediately signals that the play is aware of its own genre and inviting the audience to enjoy the theatricality, not just the story.

Costume Design: Identity in an Accessory

Costume design in this production must solve the multi-roling problem: one performer will play many roles, so each role must be instantly readable from a limited set of accessories. The base layer — typically a neutral Victorian-inflected suit in grey or cream — stays constant. Over it, a pith helmet signals India; a captain’s peaked cap and a slightly maritime posture signals the ship; a sheepskin hat and heavier coat signals the American West.

Signifier costume strategy means the designer must choose accessories that read clearly from every audience sightline (critical in in-the-round staging) and that can be donned and shed in seconds. The choice of colour is also important for character identity: Fogg’s costume is typically a consistent, precise dark grey or navy — the visual equivalent of his personality. Passepartout, by contrast, might have a slightly more bohemian base layer and brighter accessories to signal his continental exuberance.

As a lighting designer for the moment when the company begins burning the ship’s wooden deck for fuel, you might build from a cool steel-blue wash (open Atlantic, night-time) and introduce a warm orange-red flicker from below stage level — using floor-level lanterns or footlights — to suggest the growing fire. The juxtaposition of cold blue above and warm orange below creates a visual instability that mirrors the desperation of the moment. A slow, pulsing rhythm to the flicker (rather than a frantic strobe) keeps the audience in the drama rather than pulling them into a safety-concern.

As a sound designer, you might layer a low, continuous drone beneath the scene — representing the ship’s engines slowing — with the distant crack and hiss of timber burning. Non-diegetic underscore could begin quietly here: a single, sustained string note that rises very gradually in pitch as the fire takes hold, cueing the audience that something important is at stake without spelling it out.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark designer question, the most frequent error is to give one vague idea per discipline (“I would use interesting lighting”) without naming specific elements or explaining their effect. You must name the lantern type (profile, Fresnel, flood, gobo), the colour or gel, the direction and the effect it creates for the audience at that exact moment. For this play in particular, remember that the minimal set means light is doing the job of scenery — your lighting choices are location choices as well as mood choices. For the 20-mark extended staging response, cover all four design disciplines (set, lighting, sound, costume) AND performer choices, anchoring every point to the named moment in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Minimal scenography is a creative strength, not a limitation: the audience co-creates each location, lighting transitions replace scene changes, and every design choice carries double duty (mood and geography simultaneously).
  • Lighting is the primary scenic tool in this production — wash colours, gobos and profile lanterns each communicate a specific geographic location or emotional state without a single piece of scenery being added.
  • Costume design uses a signifier strategy: a base layer plus rapidly changed accessories lets multi-roling performers shift character in seconds while maintaining consistent identity for the principal characters.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Comic Precision and Ensemble Trust
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Fogg, Passepartout and the ensemble in the play's key moments.
lessons.content_html:
The Performer’s Challenge in This Play

No other play on the GCSE set-play list asks more of its performers in terms of physical range. An actor in Around the World in 80 Days may spend one scene as a Reform Club gentleman, the next as an elephant’s front legs, the next as a Yokohama acrobat, and the next as a ship’s captain. Each role requires a distinct physical life — a different physical quality, different proxemics to other performers, a different relationship to the audience. And they must be able to set one down and pick up another in seconds.

This lesson focuses on how to analyse and generate specific performer choices for GCSE exam questions. The key discipline is always the same: translate emotion and character into concrete vocal and physical specifics. Not “Fogg is cold” but “Fogg stands with his weight evenly distributed, spine erect, hands clasped precisely behind his back, gaze level — he does not shift his weight even when Passepartout collides with a customs official.” Not “Passepartout is excitable” but “his centre of gravity is higher than Fogg’s, his movements initiated from the chest rather than the pelvis, his gestures preceding his words by half a beat.”

Key Fact

Fogg’s defining performance quality is stillness: he is the fixed point around which every comic catastrophe revolves. Passepartout’s defining quality is kinetic expressiveness: his body registers everything, instantly. This contrast is not accidental — it is the engine of the play’s comedy.

Playing Fogg: Stillness as Performance

A common student misconception is that Fogg is a comedic character who “acts funny.” The opposite is true. Fogg is the straight man. His comedy emerges from his absolute refusal to react — his deadpan precision is the setup that allows everyone else’s reactions to land. A performer playing Fogg must train themselves to do less: to resist the impulse to react physically, to maintain an even vocal pitch and measured pace even when the scene around them is comic chaos.

In the Reform Club opening, a performer might embody Fogg’s precision by moving only when necessary — each step deliberate, placed as if measured. His gestus (in the Brechtian sense) would be one of meticulous order: he consults his pocket watch not with anxiety but with the calm certainty of a man who believes the universe should conform to his timetable. Vocally, his delivery is measured and even-paced — perhaps a received pronunciation accent delivered at a consistent mid-pitch with minimal variation in volume. He does not rise at the ends of sentences.

As a performer playing Fogg in the moment when he makes the wager with the Reform Club gentlemen, you might choose a slow turn to face the doubters — the full turn taking two counts, unhurried — then a pause of equal length before speaking. Your volume would remain exactly the same as in normal conversation: Fogg does not need to raise his voice to assert dominance. The physical choice of keeping both hands visible and still (not gripping the table, not pointing) communicates total control. Your gaze goes to each face in turn, for precisely the same amount of time, as if ticking off a checklist. This staging choice places Fogg downstage centre in the audience’s field of attention, while the ensemble’s more agitated physical life frames him from all sides, making his stillness more emphatic by contrast.

As a lighting designer for this moment, you might isolate Fogg in a tight spotlight using a profile lantern from directly above while the Reform Club ensemble is lit in a cooler, softer flood. The result is that the audience’s eye is drawn to Fogg’s face and the slight catch of light on his pocket watch — a design choice that underlines his centrality to the story without any camera cut.

Playing Passepartout: Kinetic Engagement

Passepartout is the audience’s emotional proxy — the character who visibly feels everything that Fogg refuses to show. A performer playing Passepartout must master a high-energy physical vocabulary: quick transitions of weight, responsive facial expression, a comedy timing that relies on beat and pause as much as action. His comedy often depends on the delayed reaction: he looks at the audience a half-second after something impossible has happened, sharing his disbelief with them before turning back to Fogg.

Vocally, Passepartout’s French accent is a comic resource (the play is aware of the “excitable Frenchman” cliché and leans into it while giving him genuine warmth). A performer might use a wider pitch range than Fogg — from low conspiratorial mutter to high yelp within a single speech — and a faster default pace that slows only for dramatic effect. In the Hong Kong opium-house sequence, the physical collapse into disorientation requires a performer who can shed their usual body-organisation and move with genuine chaos while remaining technically in control.

Key Fact

Passepartout’s comedy depends on a high centre of gravity, rapid weight transitions and a generous use of audience-facing gesture. He is the play’s emotional thermometer — when the audience sees his face register something, they know how to feel.

Ensemble Work: Trust and Precision

For scenes requiring ensemble lifts and contact work, the company must develop deep physical trust. In the India sequence, when performers form the body of an elephant, any collapse in coordination collapses the fiction. The precision is similar to that required of a circus troupe or a ballet corps — but in this play it must appear effortless, as if the whole company has been doing this for years.

Crowd scenes present a different challenge: blocking a group of eight performers who are each playing multiple roles requires every individual to know exactly where they are at every moment, what their sightline offers the audience, and how their body reads from all angles — particularly important in in-the-round staging. A performer playing a Reform Club gentleman is framing Fogg from one side; as soon as the scene shifts, they must re-enter as a new character from a different part of the stage, taking a new spatial relationship to the action.

Performers in this production must switch vocal quality as rapidly as they switch physical identity. A helpful toolkit: for a British customs official, a clipped, nasal received pronunciation with staccato rhythm; for an Indian elephant-driver (in brief dialogue), a specific tonal warmth and rhythmic pattern distinct from British English; for the Yokohama crowd, fragmented exclamatory sounds rather than fully formed sentences. The key exam principle is that each vocal choice must be specific and must be justified by character context. Vague answers (“I would speak in a foreign accent”) score poorly. Specific answers (“I would deliver the conductor’s three lines in a rapid, high-pitched staccato with a sharp consonant attack, suggesting official authority and impatience”) score well.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark performer question, the most common error is to describe the character’s emotional state (“Fogg would feel calm”) without translating it into specific vocal and physical choices for a named moment. You must identify the moment by name, then give at least one vocal choice (pitch, pace, volume, accent, pause) and at least one physical choice (posture, gesture, weight, centre of gravity, proxemics) with a justification for how each choice communicates meaning to the audience. For the 12-mark question on intentions, remember to explain why Eason constructed the Fogg/Passepartout contrast — what is the audience intended to feel, and what does the contrast reveal about the play’s themes?
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fogg’s stillness is not a lack of performance — it is a precisely executed choice; his refusal to react is the engine of the play’s comedy and must be described in specific physical terms (spine, weight, pace, pitch) in exam answers.
  • Passepartout’s kinetic expressiveness serves as the audience’s emotional proxy; his physical vocabulary (high centre of gravity, responsive facial expression, beat and pause comedy timing) must be as precisely described as Fogg’s restraint.
  • Ensemble work in this play demands physical trust and precision equivalent to a circus or dance company; blocking, sightlines and spatial awareness are all essential performer skills for a production staged in the round.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in constructing Passepartout as the audience's emotional proxy throughout the play. How does his performance function communicate meaning to the audience?

Identifies that his multi-roling also gives him a unique relationship with the audience: he can step in and out of minor roles and return to Passepartout without the audience losing track because his physical signature is unmistakable. practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the Hong Kong opium-house sequence to communicate Passepartout's physical and emotional disorientation. Discuss your performer direction, blocking, lighting and sound choices and their effect on the audience.

Every choice has a named effect on the audience. A directorial statement about what the audience is intended to feel.
